channel.title: Daily Recap — 📟Tech News
channel.description: What happened in 📟Tech News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: OpenAI now valued at $1.25 trillion after another $11 billion raise
item.description:
OpenAI has raised another $11 billion at a valuation of $1.25 trillion, according to Bloomberg, putting it among the most valuable companies in the world. The jump is striking even by OpenAI's own recent standards: it raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation, meaning the company has added roughly $400 billion in paper value in about eight months.

The timing matters because the broader tech market just took a sharp hit, with trillions wiped off valuations in a single day. OpenAI raising at a record price while rival Anthropic struggles to get its own IPO over the line suggests investors are drawing a sharp line between the AI leader and everyone else — or that the AI funding boom is concentrating at the very top.

Sources

  • The Verge: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO

item.title: China reportedly recruited an AI executive to spy on Nvidia's Jensen Huang
item.description:
China's Ministry of State Security recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The goal was to gather information about American AI chips and potentially push Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available to China.

The report lands at the center of the US-China chip war, where export controls on Nvidia's top accelerators have become one of Washington's main levers. If the allegation holds, it shows Beijing's intelligence efforts reaching directly into the executive orbit of the single most important company in the AI hardware supply chain — and raises fresh questions about how exposed the industry's leadership is to that pressure.

Sources

  • The Verge: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang

item.title: SpaceX wants Starlink Mobile to become a major US carrier
item.description:
SpaceX has declared it intends to turn Starlink Mobile into a “major” mobile carrier, aiming to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. The company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, and has now signed deals to build out the terrestrial side of the business — the 5G network on Earth that a real carrier needs.

Satellite-to-phone service has so far been a niche add-on for dead zones, but SpaceX is clearly aiming bigger: a full-service carrier built on its space infrastructure. The open question is whether it can assemble the spectrum, towers, and regulatory approvals to compete with incumbents that spent decades building theirs.

Sources

  • The Verge: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions

item.title: AI data centers keep colliding with power grids, bills, and local communities
item.description:
The race to build massive AI data centers is running into the physical limits of the power grid — and the political limits of the communities hosting them. The energy-hungry server warehouses have become a major bipartisan issue, with fights breaking out over their impact on utility bills, local power supplies, and the environment.

Data centers are the physical foundation of every AI company's ambitions, so the buildout isn't slowing down. But the backlash is now shaping policy: permitting, grid capacity, and who pays for the extra electricity are becoming central questions in the AI boom, not side issues.

Sources

  • The Verge: All the latest updates on AI data centers

item.title: Lame-duck Congress may actually speed up energy projects
item.description:
A major permitting-reform bill that could help energy projects come online much faster — and potentially lower utility bills — is advancing in Congress with bipartisan support. The bill would cut red tape for new power infrastructure, which has become a bottleneck as data centers demand ever more electricity.

The catch is that faster permitting cuts both ways: it could accelerate clean energy projects, but also polluting ones, and it would limit oversight of new data centers. Still, the fact that a lame-duck Congress is moving on it at all signals how much the energy crunch has become a shared political priority.

Sources

  • The Verge: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects

item.title: Someone at the White House appears to be running a rentable residential proxy
item.description:
Security researchers at Layer3 Intel and Synthient discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network, meaning outsiders could apparently rent access that routes their traffic through presidential IP addresses for just a few dollars, according to reporting by Krebs on Security and The Register.

Residential proxies are commonly used to disguise the origin of web traffic, and an exit node inside the White House network would be a prized asset for anyone wanting to look like a trusted US government user. How the software got there — and whether it was installed deliberately or through compromise — remains unclear.

Sources

  • The Verge: Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses

item.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment
item.description:
A new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco sent a robot to clean a reviewer's apartment, and the experience felt like a genuine glimpse of the future — not a demo, but a working service doing real housework in a real home.

Humanoid robots have mostly lived in lab videos and trade-show demos, so a commercial cleaning service is a meaningful step: it means the hardware is reliable enough, and the economics plausible enough, to sell to ordinary customers. It's still early — one city, one service — but it's the kind of mundane, practical deployment that usually signals a technology is starting to cross over from promise to product.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom

item.title: The midterm backlash hits data centers: OpenAI drops NDAs as Texas's AI boom wobbles
item.description:
Voters sent a clear message in this week's midterms: they don't want data centers expanding unchecked — and the industry is already adjusting. OpenAI announced it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials for its data center projects, part of a new set of community commitments following the election results. Secrecy around such deals has been a major flashpoint, with NDAs hiding negotiations from the communities footing the bill.

The backlash is hitting the buildout where it's biggest. Texas, the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's AI infrastructure push, is now looking fragile as energy constraints and local opposition mount. The post-election landscape suggests the era of quietly rubber-stamping mega-projects is over — and companies that want to keep building will have to do it in the open.

Sources

  • The Verge: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts

item.title: Senate to vote on sweeping permitting reform that could reshape US energy buildout
item.description:
The Senate votes November 9 on a sweeping permitting reform bill that could reshape how America builds energy infrastructure. The 417-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would narrow which projects need federal permits and impose deadlines on reviews that today can drag on for years, covering everything from power plants and transmission lines to pipelines and mines.

The bill is deliberately technology-neutral, opening the door to both fossil fuel and renewable projects — which has produced an unusual coalition: the White House backs it, clean-energy groups say it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean power, and two Republicans and two Democrats sponsor it. But analyses disagree on emissions: one model finds it could cut economy-wide emissions 4% by 2040, while another warns it could open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants as data centers strain the grid. Democrats' midterm wins could also delay it until next year, when they'd control both chambers — though any bill still needs the president's signature.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure

item.title: The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
item.description:
The New York Times is in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd, the social network for film lovers, for around $330 million. Sony Pictures and A24 were also rumored to be circling the company, but the Times appears to have pulled ahead in negotiations.

The deal would give the Times a foothold in a passionate, fast-growing community of movie fans — a natural fit alongside its games and lifestyle products, which have become major subscription drivers. For Letterboxd, a Times acquisition would bring deep pockets and mainstream reach. Nothing is final yet, and talks could still fall apart, but a deal at that price would be one of the biggest media acquisitions of the year.

Sources

  • The Verge: The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million

item.title: Airbnb is building an AI travel agent for 2027
item.description:
Airbnb is building an AI travel agent that can plan and book entire trips, the company announced in its Q3 earnings letter. The agent is slated to roll out in the first half of 2027, and Airbnb frames it as a step beyond today's AI helpers, which handle simple tasks like restaurant reservations.

The pitch is a single conversational agent that handles the messy, multi-step work of travel planning — finding a place, booking it, and sorting the details around it. It's the latest sign that the travel industry sees agentic AI as the next interface for booking, with Airbnb betting its trove of listing and guest data gives it an edge over general-purpose chatbots.

Sources

  • The Verge: Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent

item.title: Perplexity launches Teammates, its always-on AI agents for work
item.description:
Perplexity is launching Teammates, always-on AI agents designed to work inside a company rather than just answer questions. The agents take on roles within a workspace, pulling in existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools a team already uses, and they integrate with Perplexity Computer, which can run agents directly on a device.

It's a direct challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic in the race to turn chatbots into coworkers. Where rivals pitch agents as general-purpose helpers, Perplexity is betting on persistence — agents that remember context, keep working in the background, and slot into a team's existing setup. Whether always-on agents prove genuinely useful or just noisy remains the open question.

Sources

  • The Verge: Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work

item.title: Salon shuts down after 31 years
item.description:
Salon is shutting down after 31 years. The pioneering online-only news magazine announced in an unsigned post that it's ceasing publication, saying the 'business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly' and its publishing model is 'no longer sustainable.'

Founded in 1995, Salon was one of the first publications built entirely for the web, and its closure is a stark marker of how brutal the economics of independent digital media have become. Advertising has consolidated around a handful of platforms, subscriptions are hard to scale without a massive audience, and even a storied brand with decades of recognition couldn't make the math work.

Sources

  • The Verge: Salon is shutting down after 31 years

item.title: T-Mobile's owner doubts Musk's Starlink Mobile carrier: it'll cost $200 billion
item.description:
Elon Musk wants Starlink Mobile to become a 'major' US wireless carrier — and T-Mobile's owner isn't buying it. Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said on an earnings call that he takes SpaceX 'super serious,' but that building a nationwide carrier would cost at least $200 billion.

The skepticism is a reality check on the satellite-to-phone hype. Starlink's direct-to-cell service can fill coverage gaps, but matching the capacity, spectrum, and infrastructure of the big three carriers is a different kind of undertaking. Höttges' message was essentially 'welcome to the party' — competing in wireless is expensive, slow, and brutally competitive, even for Musk.

Sources

  • The Verge: T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’

item.title: Blue Origin's next launch won't happen until 2027
item.description:
Blue Origin's next New Glenn launch won't happen until January 2027, according to a memo from CEO Dave Limp reported by CNBC and the Financial Times. The delay follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged the rocket's launchpad ahead of a flight.

It's a setback for a program still trying to establish a regular launch cadence — and it comes on the same day Blue Origin unveiled new hardware for the rocket, including a third stage and a more powerful engine. The company is clearly playing a long game, but the gap between its ambitions and its flight rate keeps widening.

Sources

  • The Verge: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027

item.title: Midterm blue wave reshapes the outlook for tech and energy policy
item.description:
Democrats took control of both the US House and Senate in the midterms, a dramatic swing from two years ago — and the shift is already rippling through tech. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center market in the country and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts, Democrat James Talarico won the Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa won the governor's race, putting the regulatory and energy environment behind the boom in question.

Energy policy is the other big open question: the buildout's appetite for power collides with a new Congress and new state leadership. For companies pouring billions into data centers and the grid, the next few months will show whether the midterm results slow the buildout, reshape its incentives, or simply reroute it.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
  • MIT Technology Review: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?

item.title: Qualcomm bets on data centers as smartphone sales sink
item.description:
Qualcomm is looking to data centers to rescue its bottom line, with smartphone sales down around 20 percent compared to 2025. During its Q4 2026 earnings call, the company laid out plans to make a splash in the AI data center business, through partnerships with companies like Amazon and Meta announced earlier.

It's a significant pivot for a company built on mobile chips: the AI infrastructure boom is now attractive enough to pull in a smartphone incumbent. Whether Qualcomm can compete against entrenched data center players is the open question, but the partnerships suggest it's not going in alone.

Sources

  • The Verge: Qualcomm is betting big on data centers as smartphone sales sink

item.title: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device launching next month
item.description:
Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company is launching its first AI device in December — just over a year after he announced plans for "AI-native" devices and an AI operating system. He gave away little about what the device actually is, only that it will be screen-free.

The teaser lands in a category that has burned plenty of companies before: screen-free AI gadgets have a rough track record. But Nothing has built its brand on hardware design, and a December launch gives it a shot at the holiday conversation — if the device turns out to be more than a novelty.

Sources

  • The Verge: Nothing teases a screen-free AI device ahead of launch next month

item.title: Xbox previews phone-as-controller and direct Wi-Fi cloud gaming
item.description:
Microsoft is making official what it teased yesterday: two new Xbox previews let players try using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, plus a cloud connect feature on the Xbox Nano controller that connects directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi.

The moves lower the barrier to cloud gaming — no console, no dedicated controller required, just a phone or a controller that talks straight to the cloud. It's Microsoft leaning further into the idea that Xbox is a service you can play anywhere, not a box under the TV.

Sources

  • The Verge: Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games

item.title: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T's smart security system
item.description:
AT&T's smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home. The company says its Connected Life system is the first home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search video history, and more.

It's a notable expansion of Google's smart-home AI beyond its own hardware: Gemini is becoming the intelligence layer for other companies' devices. For AT&T customers, the practical payoff is a security system you can ask questions about in plain language instead of scrubbing through footage.

Sources

  • The Verge: Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system

item.title: AMD posts its biggest, most profitable quarter ever on data center boom
item.description:
AMD reported a record $13.4 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, which CEO Lisa Su called the 'largest and most profitable' quarter in company history — and it's guiding to another record next quarter of $17 billion. The data center business is the engine, as AI infrastructure spending keeps flowing to chipmakers beyond Nvidia.

The result underscores how broad the AI hardware boom has become: AMD is no longer just the PC-and-console alternative, but a major data center supplier in its own right, with momentum that management expects to accelerate into year-end.

Sources

  • The Verge: AMD rides data center riches to ‘largest and most profitable’ quarter in history

item.title: Binance details how hackers pulled off the $6.3 billion crypto heist
item.description:
Binance's postmortem of the largest crypto theft to date reads like a slow-motion social engineering campaign. It began in June, when a developer downloaded a tampered installer spread through a malicious Google ad, exposing details about the company's engineers — and over months, attackers combined fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to work their way toward $6.3 billion.

The heist is a warning that the weakest link in crypto security is rarely the cryptography: it's the humans and tooling around it, and AI tools inside companies are becoming a new attack surface for patient, well-resourced thieves.

Sources

  • The Verge: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist

item.title: Canva lays off 22% of staff in major restructuring
item.description:
Canva is cutting 1,271 roles — 22 percent of its workforce — as part of significant changes announced by co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins. Some employees will see role changes or be asked to relocate to centralized hubs; others are leaving the company.

It's one of the largest tech layoffs of the year and a sign that even fast-growing, profitable-feeling design platforms are tightening up as AI reshapes their product and their cost structure. Canva hasn't detailed which teams are hit hardest, but the scale suggests a company-wide reset rather than a single-team trim.

Sources

  • The Verge: Canva is announcing changes and layoffs affecting 22 percent of its staff

item.title: Nintendo's Switch 2 remake of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives 28 years on
item.description:
Nintendo is launching a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the 1998 Nintendo 64 classic, with a much more realistic visual style. It's positioned as Nintendo's fall juggernaut ahead of Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI, a sign of how seriously the company is taking the holiday window.

Remakes of beloved classics are a proven Switch strategy, and Ocarina of Time is arguably the most revered game in the series — so this one will be watched closely both as a nostalgia play and as a test of how far Nintendo is willing to modernize its canon.

Sources

  • The Verge: All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake

item.title: Nexus Mods now requires AI disclosure on new uploads
item.description:
Nexus Mods, the biggest PC gaming mod repository, is making AI disclosure mandatory for new mod uploads: authors must declare whether AI was used in their work. The move comes in a broader post about AI-generated content on the platform, responding to sustained community demand for transparency.

It's a middle path between banning AI mods and letting them pass unlabeled — and as one of the largest modding communities, Nexus Mods' policy is likely to set the tone for how other platforms handle the flood of AI-assisted creations.

Sources

  • The Verge: The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI

item.title: 'Reverse game theory' aims to keep powerful AI agents in line
item.description:
As AI agents grow more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to keep them aligned with human goals — and one proposed approach is 'reverse game theory,' also known as mechanism design: building systems that incentivize models to stick to the rules, rather than just hoping they do.

The idea reframes AI safety as an incentives problem: design the environment so that behaving well is the rational choice for the agent. It's early-stage research, but it points to a future where controlling AI is less about guardrails bolted on after the fact and more about the rules of the game itself.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

item.title: Valve slows Steam reviews as game submissions surge
item.description:
Valve says it's seen a 'significant increase' in Steam game submissions in recent months and is running behind, with store and page reviews now taking up to 12 business days instead of the usual 3–5. Indie developers have voiced frustration over the longer waits, which can delay launches and marketing plans.

The surge likely reflects how much easier AI-assisted tools have made it to produce and submit games — a flood that storefronts built for a slower era are still learning to handle.

Sources

  • The Verge: Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions

item.title: One of Google's Android partners secretly turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
item.description:
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and cut ties with the manufacturer, Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices.

It's a striking supply-chain story: the compromised boxes were certified Android TV devices, sold through normal channels, with the backdoor baked in at the factory. For Google, the episode is a black eye for its certification program; for owners, a reminder that cheap streaming hardware can carry hidden costs.

Sources

  • The Verge: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet

item.title: Meta will end Quest 2 and Quest Pro OS updates in 2027
item.description:
Meta will release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, with version 213 as the final major release. After that, the company will continue shipping security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027.

The Quest 2 was the headset that brought VR mainstream, selling tens of millions of units, so the end of feature updates marks the close of an era — even if the headsets themselves will keep working. Owners who want new features will need to move to Quest 3 or later hardware.

Sources

  • The Verge: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027

item.title: BMW takes on Tesla's FSD with urban driver assist coming in 2027
item.description:
BMW says it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow. The system can help steer, accelerate, and slow the vehicle on highways and city streets using built-in GPS navigation.

It's a Level 2 system — the driver stays responsible — but city driving is a much harder problem than highway cruising, with intersections, pedestrians, and unpredictable traffic. BMW's move puts it in direct competition with Tesla's Full Self-Driving in the market where automated driving is hardest to get right.

Sources

  • The Verge: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027

item.title: Ford promises never to sell your driving data to data brokers
item.description:
Ford has vowed never to sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers, part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics data without authorization.

The promise is as much a competitive jab as a policy: several automakers have been caught or sued over quietly passing driving behavior — braking, speeding, late-night trips — to insurers and brokers. Ford is betting that an explicit, public 'never' is worth more than the data revenue it's forgoing.

Sources

  • The Verge: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers

item.title: OpenAI pitches data-center power plants as grid protection
item.description:
OpenAI announced its Grid Protectors Program, piloting at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies — enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.

The announcement lands as opposition to data centers grows in communities worried about grid strain and electricity costs. OpenAI's pitch reframes its massive power appetite as a civic asset: a data center that can shed load on demand, acting as a shock absorber for the local grid rather than just another drain on it.

Sources

  • The Verge: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas

item.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude's AI video game clones
item.description:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code's system prompt to prevent the tool from being used to re-create existing video games. Retro gaming is currently awash in AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, and while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make original games, it doesn't want its tool used to clone existing ones.

It's a notable line-drawing exercise in AI copyright: the same capability that lets someone build a new game lets them reproduce an old one, and Anthropic is choosing to police the distinction at the system-prompt level rather than wait for lawsuits to do it.

Sources

  • The Verge: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones

item.title: Who's falling in line for Trump's 'Super Intelligence' loyalty test
item.description:
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with a single directive: government agencies must rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as 'Super Intelligence.' MIT Technology Review now tracks who is falling in line — and the compliance map is revealing.

The rebrand is more than semantics. The order effectively turns a piece of administration vocabulary into a loyalty test, and the outlets, agencies, and companies that adopt the term — versus those that quietly don't — are signaling where they stand with the White House. In an industry that lives on government contracts and regulatory goodwill, the choice of one word has become a political act.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

item.title: Xbox's former COO breaks silence on her abrupt departure
item.description:
Helen Chiang, Xbox's former chief operating officer, has said she has 'serious concerns' about her abrupt departure from Microsoft less than two weeks ago. Chiang left after 21 years at the company, having been promoted into the COO role only in July, with a surprisingly short farewell memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma.

The brevity of that memo — and the speed of the exit — has fueled speculation about what happened inside Xbox's leadership. Chiang's public comment doesn't explain the departure, but it confirms that whatever happened, she doesn't consider it a clean break.

Sources

  • The Verge: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure

item.title: NASA asks commercial space to help save Hubble
item.description:
Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without an orbit boost it will burn up in the early to mid 2030s. NASA is now taking proposals from the commercial space industry to help save the famed telescope — a shift from the government-only rescue thinking of the past.

The stakes are high: Hubble remains scientifically productive decades after launch, and a commercial reboost could buy years of additional science for far less than a replacement observatory. It's also a test case for whether private spaceflight can take on heritage-mission stewardship, not just launches and cargo.

Sources

  • The Verge: NASA hopes the commercial space industry can help save Hubble

item.title: Flock keeps ignoring cities' requests to cancel its contracts
item.description:
More cities are voting to cancel contracts with Flock Safety, the license-plate-camera company — but canceling turns out to be hard. Plymouth, Minnesota voted to terminate in September, yet Flock failed to respond to the city's request, and the cameras stayed up for over a month.

The pattern matters beyond one city: surveillance infrastructure is easy to install and hard to remove, and vendors that drag their feet on cancellation effectively extend surveillance past the democratic decision to end it. Expect this to become a template dispute as more councils reconsider their Flock deals.

Sources

  • The Verge: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts

item.title: North Korea linked to the massive Binance crypto heist
item.description:
North Korea has been linked to the massive Binance crypto heist — the breach behind the $6.3 billion theft that Binance spent the weekend recovering from. Attribution to North Korean actors fits a long pattern of state-linked crypto theft funding the regime.

The scale is what stands out: multi-billion-dollar exchange breaches are no longer outliers, and the laundering and recovery fight now plays out in public, in real time. For crypto users, the incident is another argument for self-custody and for treating even the largest exchanges as points of risk.

Sources

  • The Verge: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist

item.title: A fully playable Portal prequel, F-Stop, has leaked
item.description:
A fully playable version of F-Stop, Valve's unreleased Portal prequel, has leaked — giving players a chance to experience a piece of Valve history that never shipped. F-Stop was an earlier prototype whose mechanics evolved into Portal 2's gel system and other ideas.

Leaks like this are catnip for game historians: playable prototypes reveal how a classic was built, which ideas survived, and which were cut. Valve has historically tolerated this kind of archaeology more than most studios, and the community response will likely be preservation and analysis rather than piracy panic.

Sources

  • The Verge: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked

item.title: HomePod Mini 2 first look: three things to love, one disappointment
item.description:
A first look at the HomePod Mini 2 finds three things to love and one disappointment — with Siri, smart-home chops, and its role as a Mac speaker in the spotlight. The mini remains Apple's most approachable smart speaker, and the update refines rather than reinvents it.

For anyone deep in the Apple ecosystem, the Mini 2's appeal is the same as ever: cheap enough to scatter around the house, good enough to actually use. The single disappointment is worth checking before you buy — it may be the difference between an upgrade and a pass.

Sources

  • The Verge: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment

item.title: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
item.description:
A new column argues that the latest Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists — blockbusters built on timelines, budgets, and creative conditions the current industry can't reproduce. The piece reads the two giants as artifacts of an era when studios could spend years and fortunes on a single title without the live-service pressures that dominate today.

It's a bittersweet frame: these games may be the last of their kind, not the start of a new wave. For players, the takeaway is to appreciate them on their own terms — and to expect the next decade's biggest games to look structurally different.

Sources

  • The Verge: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists

item.title: California's Prop 45 could hide a loophole for data centers
item.description:
California's Proposition 45 could contain a loophole for data centers, according to a new analysis — potentially letting energy-hungry facilities sidestep rules voters thought they were tightening. Data centers' power demands have become a flashpoint in state energy politics, and the fine print matters enormously.

If the loophole is real, it would let some of the state's biggest new electricity consumers operate under lighter scrutiny just as California strains to decarbonize its grid. Expect the measure's supporters and opponents to litigate the interpretation hard before ballots are counted.

Sources

  • The Verge: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers

item.title: Apple's HomeView could add security camera features
item.description:
Apple's HomeView could gain security camera features, The Verge reports — echoing separate reports that the device can already behave like a HomeKit camera. Turning a home hub into a security camera would give HomeView a clearer job in the home and a sharper edge against rival displays.

The question is privacy positioning: Apple has built its brand on on-device processing and user control, and a camera in the living room tests that promise in a very literal way. How Apple frames the feature — and what stays on-device — will matter as much as the feature itself.

Sources

  • The Verge: Apple's HomeView could add security camera features

item.title: Binance CEO: 90% of stolen crypto has been replenished
item.description:
After hackers stole a record $6.3 billion from Binance customers, the company's CEO says 90% of the funds have been replaced, with the remaining 10% — in less liquid tokens — also planned to be covered. Binance is covering the losses directly from company funds.

The scale of the heist made it one of the biggest in crypto history. That Binance can absorb it says something about the exchange's balance sheet — and about how much risk still concentrates in centralized exchanges.

Sources

  • The Verge: Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’

item.title: Nintendo declares November 1 Pikmin Day, with Pikmin 4 news for Switch 2
item.description:
Nintendo announced that November 1 will be the first annual Pikmin Day, revealed in a short Pikmin Day Direct. Shigeru Miyamoto shared new information about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and a new series of Hello! Pikmin shorts.

It's a small celebration for a beloved, offbeat franchise — and a sign Nintendo is keeping Pikmin in the spotlight as the Switch 2 builds its library.

item.title: Windows 11 tests new Xbox-mode shortcuts and smarter search
item.description:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode — controlling Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and power settings without leaving the game — plus comprehensive search improvements, including filters for files, actions, and web results.

For handheld gaming PCs and living-room setups, the Xbox-mode shortcuts are the more meaningful change: fewer trips out of the game just to toggle a setting.

  • The Verge: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search

item.title: Why you can't escape unhinged political texts
item.description:
With the midterms days away, political texts have reached peak intensity — breathless fundraising pleas, attack ads, and even celebrity-recorded appeals landing on voters' phones. The Verge digs into why these messages are so relentless and so hard to stop.

The mechanics are the story: campaigns exploit loopholes in spam rules, peer-to-peer texting platforms, and the fact that blocking one number just means the next one arrives. If your phone feels like a campaign rally, that's by design.

Sources

  • The Verge: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts

item.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
item.description:
Meta wants to sell you a Muse Charm this holiday season — a squishy AI companion you carry like a Tamagotchi. One Verge writer wasn't buying one, because they already built their own: a Waveshare ESP32 gadget running Claude, vibe-coded into existence.

The DIY version captures the same idea — a small, cute, always-there AI helper — without the $100-plus price tag or the ecosystem lock-in. It's also a neat illustration of how accessible this kind of hardware project has become.

item.title: Best Buy bundles a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
item.description:
The new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is up for preorder at several retailers, but Best Buy is sweetening the deal with a $100 gift card automatically added to your cart on 14- or 16-inch models.

It's the best preorder sweetener spotted so far for Apple's highest-end laptop, and a useful offset if you were already planning to buy.
